title: Urgency, fear, and authority triggers
body_md:
## Pressure is a reason to change pace

Urgency, fear and claimed authority often arrive together. “The account closes in ten minutes,” “you will be arrested,” and “I am from the fraud team” are designed to make the proposed action seem like the only safe exit. The UK NCSC identifies authority, urgency, emotion and scarcity as common scam cues. A cue is a reason to slow down and check, not proof that every urgent situation is false. Real card alerts, medical calls and workplace deadlines exist.

The mechanism is practical: a short clock shrinks the time available to consult a second source; fear narrows attention to avoiding loss; an official-sounding title makes questions feel improper. An attacker may add secrecy (“do not tell your family”) or continuous contact (“stay on the line”) to prevent outside comparison. There is no reliable universal pause length. Take enough time to end the inbound interaction and reach the institution or person by a route you already know. A real emergency can still be handled through the real service.

Inspect the **requested remedy**, not just the threatened problem. A caller who claims fraud and then asks you to transfer money to “protect” it is offering a remedy that creates the risk. A message about an account lock that asks for a verification code has the same structure. Ask what would happen if you did nothing for a few minutes, then check in your own app, card statement, published service number or known work directory. Do not debate a caller into proving their status; their answers are part of the same unverified channel.

A legitimate deadline may be inconvenient. The independent channel may confirm that payment is due, a card is blocked, or a meeting is about to start. Once confirmed, follow the real procedure. If the pressure involves immediate physical danger, contact local emergency services by a number you know; do not delay emergency help to finish an online checklist. The cases and exercise show how to preserve both caution and urgency when the underlying issue might be real.

widget_config.goal: Respond to a fear-plus-deadline claim by verifying the problem and remedy through a known route before taking a consequential action.
widget_config.today_action: Choose one short phrase to use under pressure: “I will check this through my own app or number and call back.”
widget_config.scope: General decision rule; UK NCSC and US FTC consumer examples. Actual deadlines, emergency numbers and legal procedures depend on place and institution.

sources.title: UK NCSC — how to spot a scam message or call
sources.scope: UK public guidance, published 2021, reviewed 2022; cues and independent contact, not a diagnostic test.

sources.title: US FTC — How to Avoid a Scam
sources.scope: US consumer guidance (2023); impersonation, pressure, payment methods and independent contact.

sources.title: US FTC — unexpected calls about money at risk
sources.scope: US consumer alert (January 2026); call back using an existing card, statement, app or official site.

blocks.title: Synthetic: “protect your savings now”
blocks.situation: A caller says a fraudulent transfer is pending, claims to be a bank supervisor, and gives you eight minutes to move savings to a new “secure” account. They insist you stay on the call.
blocks.analysis: Fear, authority and a clock reinforce each other; the offered remedy is itself a transfer. End the call without moving money or reading codes. Check activity in your own bank app or call the card’s established number. Ask the real bank what protective steps it actually supports.

blocks.title: Synthetic: real card alert at a bad moment
blocks.situation: Your bank app, opened from your phone’s home screen, shows a declined transaction and a card lock. You also received a text saying the card was locked.
blocks.analysis: The alert may be genuine. The independently opened app confirms an account state, but you still follow the bank’s own in-app or card-backed instructions rather than a text link. Fast action can be appropriate after authentication.

blocks.title: The deadline call
blocks.setup: Three separate fictional housing snapshots test a deadline, a callback route and a tenant-portal finding. Each new snapshot resets the situation; no choice carries into the next one. This is not legal or housing advice.

steps.prompt: The caller cites your building and a deadline. What first?

choices.text: Pay through the link to preserve the renewal.
choices.consequence: You may pay a party you have not verified.
choices.explanation: Correct building details and a deadline do not authenticate a payment link.

choices.text: Note the claimed deadline and end the call before using any link.
choices.consequence: You make room for an independent check.
choices.explanation: You can act quickly through a trusted office route if the claim is real.

steps.prompt: Separate new call: a claimed housing-office worker says the published office line is overloaded and offers an alternate number. Which route do you use?

choices.text: Use the alternate number they supply.
choices.consequence: The same source now controls the “verification” route.
choices.explanation: An excuse about the usual channel must itself be verified.

choices.text: Open the known tenant portal or call the office number on your existing lease.
choices.consequence: You use contact details held before the call.
choices.explanation: The office can confirm whether a payment and deadline exist.

steps.prompt: Separate new renewal: you opened your known tenant portal yourself. It shows a renewal due this week but no new payment link. An inbound caller nevertheless asks you to pay through a new link. What next?

choices.text: Pay the caller anyway because the deadline is close.
choices.consequence: A real deadline can be used to attach a fake remedy.
choices.explanation: Follow the portal’s listed process or ask staff through the known channel.

choices.text: Complete any due action in the portal and ask staff about the conflicting call.
choices.consequence: You address the genuine task while rejecting the unverified payment path.
choices.explanation: This separates the real deadline from the caller’s invented instruction.

blocks.debrief: Debrief: these are three independent decisions, so a prior payment or ended call does not create the later portal finding. Urgency can accompany a real renewal, while an unverified payment link remains unsafe. Replay each snapshot and check the claimed problem and proposed remedy separately.

questions.prompt: An urgent fraud call says a “safe account” transfer is the only remedy. What do you do?

choices.explanation: A later check may not undo an authorized transfer.

choices.text: End the call and use your own bank contact to verify both problem and remedy.
choices.explanation: Correct: the caller cannot authenticate their own instructions.

questions.prompt: Your independently opened bank app confirms a card lock. Does the text alert have to be fake?

choices.text: No; use the app’s own instructions to handle the real lock.
choices.explanation: Correct: the underlying issue can be real, and the action path remains independent.

choices.text: Yes; urgent texts can never describe real account events.
choices.explanation: A text may be genuine; the app confirmation changes the evidence.

questions.prompt: Someone claims the main office line is down. What is the status of that claim?

choices.text: A reason to use their new number without checking.
choices.explanation: That keeps verification under the caller’s control.

choices.text: An unverified exception to check through an existing portal or later known contact.
choices.explanation: Correct: an exception is not evidence of its own truth.
